chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhayna, from Bureyd al-'Ijli, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) regarding the words of God, Blessed and Exalted:
But indeed We have given to the Progeny of Ibrahim the Book and the Wisdom, and We have given them a Grand Kingdom.

He said: 'He (God) made from them the Messengers, the Prophets, and the Imams. So how can they acknowledge it regarding the Progeny of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) yet deny it regarding the Progeny of Muhammad (may God bless him and his family)?'

He (the narrator) said: 'I said: "and We have given them a Grand Kingdom"?' He (the Imam) said: 'The Grand Kingdom is that He (God) made the Imams among them. Whoever obeys them obeys God, and whoever disobeys them disobeys God. Thus it is the Grand Kingdom.'

key_terms.آلَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ: Progeny of Ibrahim — the lineage through which prophethood and Imamate were transmitted
key_terms.أَئِمَّةً: Imams — divinely appointed leaders whose authority is an extension of divine command
key_terms.الْمُلْكُ الْعَظِيمُ: The Grand Kingdom — interpreted as the divine authority of the Imams, not worldly political power
key_terms.يُقِرُّونَ: Acknowledge/affirm — the rhetorical challenge of inconsistent acceptance of divine appointment

ai.seo_question: What does the Grand Kingdom given to the family of Ibrahim mean in Shia interpretation?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (a.s.) offers an authoritative commentary on Quran 4:54, explaining that the 'Grand Kingdom' given to the family of Ibrahim refers specifically to the institution of the Imamate. The Imam employs a rhetorical challenge: if people accept that God appointed Messengers, Prophets, and Imams from the progeny of Ibrahim, why do they reject the same divine pattern for the progeny of Muhammad? The Imam defines the Grand Kingdom as the Imams' divine authority, grounded in their unique position where obedience to them constitutes obedience to God Himself — a fundamental Shia doctrine of the Imamate.
